absent: The fragments do not show the implementation or failure modes of the architecture page addition helper.
The fragments do not show true online verification, zone span synchronization, or node reference counting when hotplug is enabled.
The fragments do not show reserve pool blocking waits, allocation failure handling, or bulk partial success semantics.
The fragments do not show buddy allocation, page isolation, compaction, or reclaim scanning algorithms.
The fragments do not show how generational sequences advance, how tiers are assigned, or how Bloom filters are maintained.
The fragments do not show container list management, locking order across nodes, or interrupt safety beyond the stated guards.

findings.text: A hotplug notification handler receives the descriptor of the first page in a newly onlined range plus the block order and produces no result, allowing the core to delegate per-block onlining policy.

The range addition entry accepts a node identifier, a starting frame number, a page count and an opaque hotplug parameter block, then forwards the request to the architecture helper and propagates its status.

Movable node reporting has two build configurations, one reflecting a global enable flag and one that constantly reports disabled, so callers cannot assume dynamic behavior without knowing the configuration.

In the full configuration the per-node reclaim coordination uses a sleeping mutual exclusion object embedded in the node descriptor, with separate operations to acquire, release and initialize that object around kswapd state changes.
In the reduced configuration the same three per-node reclaim coordination operations accept the node descriptor but perform no synchronization, providing source compatibility without exclusion.

The frame-to-page lookup first validates the frame number and only then converts it, otherwise yielding a null indicator. In this configuration it does not verify that the page is currently onlined or that the zone span is stable.

Zone span stability operations are disabled in this configuration, with beginning a read sequence and retrying it both constantly reporting no change, while acquiring or releasing write exclusion and initializing the sequence object have no effect.

Node onlining and hotplug reference handling are stubbed to success-like behavior, where attempting to online a node always reports success, taking or dropping online references does nothing, and bracketing a hotplug section does nothing.
Memory map placement support is constantly reported as unavailable, and the default onlining policy is constantly the offline mode, so no automatic onlining can be expected from these queries.

Node size changes are serialized by an interrupt-saving spin-style guard held in the node descriptor, with paired acquire and release operations that preserve caller interrupt state plus a one-time initializer for that guard.

When resizing support is compiled out, the same three node-size operations accept a node descriptor and flag storage but perform no locking or initialization, so they must not be relied on for exclusion.

Offline and removal paths are disabled, with requesting node offline doing nothing and discarding its result, offlining a page range reporting invalid argument, removing by address reporting busy, forced removal by address doing nothing, and range-based offline plus removal reporting busy.

The allocation handler receives allocation flags plus backend state and returns an element pointer, while the release handler receives an element plus backend state and returns nothing. The pool descriptor itself combines a short-term exclusion object, a configured minimum depth, a live spare count, a table holding spare elements, opaque backend state, and a queue for waiters blocked on empty reserves.

A pool counts as initialized exactly when its spare table is present, and as saturated when its observed live spare count reaches or exceeds its configured minimum, using a single atomic-style read for the live count.

Pool lifecycle and fast paths are provided as allocation-tracking wrappers around internal constructors and allocators, including initialization of an embedded descriptor, node-aware creation with flags and placement, default creation on the kernel placement, single and bulk allocation, plus a no-reserve path that directly invokes the backend allocator.

Typed convenience wrappers bind the generic pool to slab caches, sized heap blocks, or paged extents by preselecting matching allocation and release handlers and encoding the cache pointer, byte size, or page order as opaque backend state for both init and create forms.
Two inclusion guards provide stable preprocessor sentinels for the reserve pool header and the zone descriptor header, allowing idempotent inclusion.
The largest buddy order is ten in the default build and comes from an architecture-forced configuration value in the alternate build, so all order-derived sizes are configuration dependent.
The page count covered by the largest order is one shifted by that ceiling, alignment to that count is tested with a helper predicate, and the total number of orders is the ceiling plus one.

The pageblock order ceiling follows the buddy ceiling by default but can be overridden by configuration, while allocations beyond order three are classified as costly for reclaim and compaction heuristics.

Folio size ceilings vary by build, with one following the buddy ceiling and others deriving from section size, from sixteen gigabyte or one gigabyte boundaries minus page shift, or from the middle directory span minus page shift. The folio page count is one shifted by the active ceiling.

Optimized descriptor-map alignment is zero unless tail optimization and descriptor power-of-two sizing both hold, in which case it scales with folio size. Tail bookkeeping starts at an order derived from two pages per descriptor and clamps negative tail counts to zero.

Pageblock mobility distinguishes unmovable, movable and reclaimable classes, a count of per-CPU classes, a high-atomic reserve, an optional contiguous area, an optional isolation marker, plus end and total terminators whose numeric positions shift with configuration.

Contiguous-area testing has enabled and disabled builds, with the enabled build comparing a type value or looking up the block type of a page or folio at a frame, while the disabled build constantly reports false. Movability accepts either contiguous or movable, and mergeability accepts only types below the per-CPU boundary.

Free-list traversal nests an order loop from zero to the order count inside a type loop up to the type terminator, binding each iteration to the corresponding per-order per-type list. Block-type queries for a page or folio delegate to a frame-indexed helper using the page frame number.
Each buddy order maintains one queue head per mobility type plus a counter of free pages in that order, allowing per-type draining while tracking order totals.

Node placement statistics track intended hits, remote misses, foreign placements, interleave hits, local and other allocations, terminated by a count. An alternate build collapses that count to zero, indicating no per-item storage.

Zone counters cover free pages and free blocks, an LRU base marker, active and inactive anonymous and file classes, unevictable, write-pending, locked, optionally compressed-pool pages, contiguous free, RCU-deferred free, optionally unaccepted, closed by a terminator.

Node counters begin with an LRU base and active plus inactive anonymous and file classes plus unevictable, then reclaimable and unreclaimable slab byte counts, isolated anonymous and file temporaries, workingset node counts, and refault, activation and restoration tallies split by anonymous versus file, plus a node-reclaim tally.

The same node enumeration continues with mapped anonymous and file counts, total file pages, dirty and writeback file states, shared memory totals including transparent huge and directory-mapped components, file huge and mapped components, anonymous huge, scanning write and immediate tallies, dirtied, written and throttled-written lifetime counts, miscellaneous reclaimable kernel pages, and pin acquisition versus release counts.

The tail of the node enumeration covers virtual mapping usage, kernel stack and optional shadow stack consumption, page table and secondary table usage, optional device translation pages, optional swap cache, optional promotion success and candidate tallies, demotion and steal and scan families split by reclaimer and by anonymous versus file, rotation and refill, optional huge-table, balloon, kernel-file, and graphics activity versus reclaim pools, closed by a terminator.

Transparent huge display is enabled only when huge support is configured and then only for anonymous huge, file huge, shared huge, shared directory-mapped and file directory-mapped counters. Byte-unit reporting applies solely to the two slab byte counters, with all other indices treated as page units.

Least-recently-used numbering uses zero for the base, one for the active offset and two for the file offset, yielding inactive and active variants for anonymous and file plus unevictable and a count. Workingset accounting uses zero for anonymous, one for file and two for their joint index.

Reclaim throttling distinguishes writeback, isolated, no-progress and congested reasons closed by a count, while per-vector flags mark congestion observed by container reclaim versus node reclaim, with clearing rules that let node reclaim unthrottle container-throttled vectors but not the reverse for the root.

List iteration covers either every LRU index up to its count or only the evictable prefix through active file. File classification accepts the two file indices and activity classification accepts the two active indices.
Generational reclaim keeps at least two and at most four generations, up to four tiers per type, and a history depth that equals the maximum in full builds but collapses to one otherwise.

Generation and reference bit selections derive from width and offset parameters, with a combined flag adding the referenced bit. Type separation uses anonymous versus file, capability enumeration covers core, table-walk and non-leaf youth plus a count, and batching spans from one machine word up to sixty-four times that.

The generational folio tracker holds a monotonically advanced youngest sequence, per-type oldest sequences, per-generation creation times, lazily sorted per-generation per-type per-zone queues with eventually consistent sizes, moving averages of refaulted versus total per tier, lock-guarded protected counts plus lock-free evicted and refaulted tallies, an enable switch, membership generation and segment identifiers, and a global-reclaim linkage. Accompanying memory statistics distinguish total and young leaf entries plus filter-found versus filter-added non-leaf entries with a count.
Each address-space iteration state maintains two rotating membership filters.

Iteration state records a sequence snapshot, resume and stop list positions, rotating filters and per-history debugging tallies. The walk batch records the target vector, a possibly stale sequence, the next address, per-generation per-type per-zone promotion staging, batched statistics, a total, a reclaim inclination, and a force flag.

Container generation tracking uses three generations and eight bins per generation, with a per-node counter, per-generation container counts, per-generation per-bin queues for global reclaim, and a guarding spin-style lock.

Aging advances the youngest sequence while eviction advances per-type oldest sequences, with timestamps marking generation births and an enable flag gating the whole scheme. Protected counts require holding the LRU guard whereas evicted and refaulted tallies permit lock-free updates.

Several queries and guards become inert when their feature is compiled out, including frame lookup without online verification, sequence checks that never detect tearing, size and reclaim locks that exclude nothing, and offline or removal requests that always fail or do nothing, so callers must handle those degraded contracts.

Saturation is judged from a single unsynchronized observation that can race with concurrent allocation, and order ceilings plus folio limits plus history depths all shift with build options, so size calculations and array bounds derived from them must be treated as configuration dependent.
External one-shot read helper relied on by the saturation predicate.
External build-option query relied on for conditional counters and alignment.
External sleeping-guard initializer relied on by node reclaim setup.
External sleeping-guard acquisition relied on by node reclaim locking.
External spin-guard initializer variant relied on by node size setup.
Alternate external spin-guard initializer variant relied on by node size setup.
